lesson.title: Blocked Before It Begins: Prezygotic Barriers
lesson.summary: Prezygotic barriers are reproductive isolating mechanisms that prevent mating or fertilization from happening at all, including differences in habitat, timing, behavior, mechanical fit, and gamete compatibility.
lesson.body:
Prezygotic barriers are the first line of defense against interbreeding between species. As the name tells you, they act "before the zygote," meaning they stop reproduction at some stage before a sperm and egg ever combine. Biologists usually group prezygotic barriers into five overlapping categories, and it helps to think of them as a series of checkpoints that a potential mating has to pass through in order.

The first checkpoint is habitat isolation. Two species can live in the same general region but rarely encounter each other because they occupy different microhabitats. For example, one species of garter snake in North America hunts mainly on land while a closely related species spends most of its time in water, so even though their ranges overlap broadly, individuals of the two types rarely cross paths in a way that would lead to mating.

The second checkpoint is temporal isolation, meaning the species breed at different times. This can mean different seasons, different times of day, or even different years, as happens in periodical cicadas whose broods emerge on different multi-year cycles. A well-documented plant example involves two pine species in California, one of which releases pollen in early spring and the other in late spring, so their flowering periods barely overlap even though the trees themselves can grow in the same forests.

The third checkpoint is behavioral isolation, which relies on differences in courtship signals or mating rituals that members of one species simply do not recognize or respond to in another. This is especially well studied in songbirds and in fireflies, where each species has its own characteristic flash pattern, and females typically only respond to the pattern of their own species. Behavioral isolation is often considered one of the most important barriers in animals with elaborate courtship, because it can evolve relatively quickly as populations diverge in their signals.

The fourth checkpoint is mechanical isolation, where physical differences in reproductive structures prevent mating from being physically completed. This is common in insects with complex genitalia that function almost like a lock and key, and it also shows up in flowering plants, where a flower's shape may only allow pollination by an insect of a particular size or body shape.

The fifth and final checkpoint is gametic isolation. Even if mating happens, in species that fertilize externally (many marine invertebrates such as sea urchins) or if sperm is transferred internally, the sperm of one species may simply fail to recognize or fuse with the egg of another, because surface proteins on the gametes do not match up chemically. Sea urchins are a particularly well studied case, because researchers can mix eggs and sperm from different species in seawater and directly observe that fertilization rates drop sharply between species compared to within a species.

Notice that these barriers act in sequence, and any single one that stops reproduction is sufficient to keep gene pools separate, the later checkpoints only matter if reproduction gets past the earlier ones. This is worth connecting back to reproductive isolation as a whole: prezygotic barriers are usually considered "cheaper" for a species to rely on than postzygotic barriers, because postzygotic barriers, which you will study next, only kick in after individuals have already invested time and resources into mating and reproduction. Natural selection tends to favor the strengthening of prezygotic barriers over time in places where two related species come into contact, because individuals that waste effort on doomed matings leave fewer offspring than individuals who avoid the mismatch altogether.
